title: Fatherhood — Holding, Carrying, Teaching
hook: A child learns what a man's body means long before he learns words: from how he is held, carried, met at eye level and taught with hands.
why:
For a baby, a father is first of all a body: a chest, a pair of arms, a voice felt through a ribcage, a heartbeat, a smell. For a toddler, he is a height to be lifted to and a hand to be held. For a child, he is a pair of hands showing how a thing is done, and a body that either comes down to meet him or stays up out of reach. Long before any conversation about feelings or values, a child has learned from his father's body whether he is safe, whether he is welcome, and what men do with their hands.

This chapter is about fatherhood as a physical skill. It covers how men's bodies change when they become fathers; holding a baby, and why skin and a steady chest matter; what to do when the crying will not stop, including the one rule that must never be broken; coming down to a child's level and the cost of a still, unresponsive face; rough-and-tumble play and what it teaches; teaching with hands without taking over; and the child's right to their own body. Much of it applies to any man who cares for children: uncles, stepfathers, grandfathers, coaches and teachers.

teach.p:
It is often assumed that the biology of parenthood belongs to mothers. Research on fathers suggests that men's bodies respond as well. In a study published in 2011, Lee Gettler, Christopher Kuzawa and their colleagues followed several hundred young men in Cebu, in the Philippines, for about four and a half years. The men who became fathers during that time showed the steepest falls in testosterone, and earlier work in the same group had linked lower testosterone in fathers with more involvement in childcare.

The researchers suggested that the fall may help shift men's priorities from competing for mates toward caring for children. The study was observational, and testosterone is only one part of a complicated picture. But it challenges the idea that men are biologically sidelined in parenting. Fathers' bodies, like mothers', seem to adjust to the work.

The rest of this chapter is about that work, which is largely physical. Holding a baby, carrying a toddler on one hip while doing something with the other hand, walking at a child's pace, kneeling to tie a shoe, catching a child who jumps off a wall: fatherhood is done with the body, and children read every movement of it.

The figure here stands with a young child on his hip, the hip pushed out to take the weight, one arm wrapped under the child. It is one of the commonest postures of fathering, and from across a room it is often the first thing that marks a man as a father.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men's hormones showed no change on becoming fathers. Gettler and colleagues found a marked change, though in one population, and what it means for behaviour is still debated.

teach.p:
In a small trial published in 2007, Kerstin Erlandsson and her colleagues in Sweden studied healthy babies born by planned caesarean section, whose mothers could not hold them straight away. The babies were placed either skin to skin on their father's chest or in a cot beside him. The babies held skin to skin cried much less, and calmed down and became drowsy sooner.

The study was small, but it fits what many fathers discover: a baby held against a bare chest, hearing a heartbeat and feeling warmth and steady breathing, often settles when nothing else works. The chapter on breath in Part II described how one person's breathing can steady another's. A father's slow breath, felt through his chest, is one of the first ways a baby borrows calm.

Holding a young baby has one firm rule: support the head and neck, because for the first few months a baby cannot hold its own head up. Hold the baby close against your body, upright against your chest with a hand behind the head, or cradled in the crook of an arm.

Holding is also the start of conversation. Researchers at Harvard's Center on the Developing Child describe the back-and-forth between a baby and a caregiver, a babble answered by a voice, a look answered by a smile, as serve and return, and argue that it shapes the developing brain. The figure here holds a baby against his chest, head bowed toward it. Every sound the baby makes is a serve. A father's job is to return it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if babies held skin to skin by their fathers settled no better than babies placed in a cot. Erlandsson and colleagues found that they did, but in a trial of only 29 babies, so the result is encouraging rather than conclusive.

teach.h: When the crying will not stop.
teach.p:
All babies cry, and many cry a great deal. Crying typically increases from about two weeks of age, peaks around the second month, and eases by three to five months. Some babies cry for hours, especially in the evening, and nothing seems to help. The programme known as the Period of PURPLE Crying was developed to help parents understand that this is normal.

It is also exhausting, and exhaustion and frustration can build into something dangerous. Shaking a baby, even briefly, can cause brain damage or death. The UK programme known as ICON gives four simple messages: infant crying is normal; comforting methods can help; it is okay to walk away; never, ever shake a baby.

Walking away is the skill. If you feel anger or desperation rising, put the baby down safely on its back in a cot, leave the room, and calm yourself for a few minutes: breathe slowly, splash your face, put on music, call someone. Then go back and check on the baby. A crying baby in a safe cot is not in danger. A baby held by an adult who has lost control is.

The earlier chapters on silence and disagreement described flooding, the state of overwhelm in which thinking breaks down. A father at three in the morning with a screaming baby is a prime candidate. Learn your own signs, and step away before they peak. If the crying worries you, or you are not coping, speak to your doctor, midwife or health visitor, or a health line where you live. The figure here covers his eyes, exhausted. Every father reaches this point; what matters is what he does next.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if putting a crying baby down and stepping away were unsafe or harmful. Health services widely recommend it as a way to prevent shaking injuries, though no single study can show how many injuries it prevents.
teach.pullQuote: A crying baby in a safe cot is not in danger. A baby held by an adult who has lost control is.

teach.p:
A man standing over a small child is a giant. His face is a long way up, his voice comes from above, and his hands can reach down and lift the child whether the child wants it or not. Children read this height, and many of the simplest improvements in a father's communication come from removing it. Kneel, squat or sit so that your eyes are at the child's level, especially when they are upset, when you are setting a limit, or when you are listening to something that matters to them.

What your face does at that level matters as much as the height. In the 1970s Edward Tronick and his colleagues asked mothers to face their babies and then suddenly hold their faces still and unresponsive. Within seconds the babies tried harder to engage, then grew distressed and turned away. The procedure, known as the still face, has since been used in many studies, including with fathers. A baby needs a face that answers.

Older children need the same. A father who listens with a still face, or with his eyes on a phone, is offering a milder version of the still face, and children notice. Put the phone down, come down to their height, and let your face respond to what they are telling you.

The figures here show an adult down on one knee facing a small child, their heads level. It is one of the simplest things a father can do with his body, and one of the most powerful.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if babies showed no distress when a caregiver's face stopped responding. The still-face studies consistently find that they do; whether everyday phone use has similar effects is a reasonable inference rather than an established finding.

teach.p:
Many fathers play physically: chasing, tickling, wrestling on the floor, throwing a child in the air, piggyback rides. In 2020 Paulina Amodia-Bidakowska, Ciara Laverty and Paul Ramchandani reviewed 78 studies of father-child play carried out over four decades. They found that fathers tended to play more physically than mothers, even with very young children, and that father-child play was consistently associated with children's later ability to manage their feelings and behaviour.

The researchers were careful: the findings are correlational, so they cannot show that play causes better self-control, and mothers can play physically too. One idea is that rough play gives children an exciting, safe setting in which to practise keeping control: getting wound up and calming down, winning and losing, playing hard without hurting.

That only works if the adult keeps the play safe and fair. Research on rough-and-tumble play suggests that its benefits depend on the father being in charge of the game: setting limits, stopping when it gets too wild, not letting it tip into real aggression. And it depends on consent, as the chapter on consent described: when a child says stop, the play stops, every time, even when they are laughing.

The figure here opens his arms wide, ready to catch or to be charged at. Physical play is one of the great pleasures of fathering. Done well, it also teaches a child that strength can be gentle and that a man's power can be held in check.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if father-child play showed no association with children's self-regulation. The review found a consistent association, but in correlational studies, so play may reflect other good things in a relationship rather than cause them.

teach.p:
In 1976 David Wood, Jerome Bruner and Gail Ross watched tutors helping young children build a tricky wooden puzzle, and described what good tutoring looked like. They called it scaffolding. The tutor recruited the child's interest, simplified the task, kept the child pointed toward the goal, marked the important features, controlled frustration and demonstrated when needed, and then gradually withdrew help as the child became able to do more.

Much of scaffolding is physical. Where you put your body decides whether a child keeps the task or loses it to you. Beside the child, at their height, with your hands near the job but not on it, the child stays in charge. Behind them, with your hands over theirs, you are doing it for them. Standing over them and pointing, you are a supervisor, not a teacher.

Watch for your own frustration as the child struggles. It shows in your breath, your jaw and your hands, and children read it instantly. When you feel the urge to grab the tool and do it yourself, sit on your hands for a moment. Let the child try again. Step in with the smallest help that will work, and step out again as soon as you can.

The figures here show an adult kneeling beside a child, both facing the same task, the adult's hand near the child's but not taking over. It is the posture of a teacher who wants the child, not himself, to succeed.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if children learned as well when an adult took over the task as when an adult supported them to do it. Research on scaffolding and learning suggests they do not, though how much help is right depends on the child and the task.

teach.p:
A child learns from the earliest age whether their body belongs to them. Every time an adult stops tickling when they say stop, lets them choose a high five instead of a kiss for a visiting aunt, asks before picking them up when they are old enough to answer, or knocks before entering their room as they grow, the child learns that their no works. Every time their no is overridden, they learn the opposite.

This matters for safety. Children who know that their body is theirs, and that they can tell a trusted adult when something feels wrong, are better placed to resist and report abuse. Child-protection organisations teach exactly this, often to children of nursery age.

It also matters for sons in particular. Many fathers hug and kiss their small sons freely and then stop, somewhere around the age of eight or ten, as if affection between a man and a boy must end. The chapters on the bro hug and on touch between friends described what that does to men. Keep offering a hug, an arm across the shoulders, a hand on the back, as your son grows, and let him choose the form. You are teaching him how men touch with consent.

The figures here walk hand in hand, the adult's hand lowered to the child's height. Walking at a child's pace, with a hand they can take or let go of, is a small daily lesson in what a man's body can be: strong, steady, and on the child's terms.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if children's early experience of having their no respected made no difference to how they protected themselves later. The principle is central to child-protection guidance, though rigorous long-term evidence on its effects is limited.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Head down to a phone while the baby babbles
poseGallery.annotation: A baby's babble is a serve. Put the phone down, hold the baby close and answer with your voice and face.

poseGallery.doCaption: Beside him, at his height, hands near
poseGallery.annotation: Where you put your body decides who owns the task. Beside and level, the child keeps it; above and pointing, you take it.
To a small child, a standing man is a giant. Kneel or squat, and let your face answer what he is telling you.

caseStudy:
Kamal, thirty-three, becomes a father in October. By the sixth week, his daughter Leila cries for three or four hours every evening, and his wife is exhausted. Kamal takes the night shifts at weekends. One night at three in the morning, after two hours of walking and rocking, he feels something he has never felt before: a hot surge of anger at a tiny screaming person. It frightens him. He remembers the leaflet from the hospital. He lays Leila on her back in her cot, walks into the kitchen, runs cold water over his wrists and breathes until the anger drains. Five minutes later he goes back. She is still crying, and he is calm. He takes his shirt off and holds her against his chest, and after a while she sleeps.

He tells the health visitor about the anger, expecting to be judged. She tells him that what he did was exactly right.

Three years later Kamal is teaching Leila to ride a bike. His instinct is to grip the handlebars and run alongside steering. He makes himself let go of the bars and jog beside her with a hand hovering near her back, not touching. She wobbles, falls, cries, and gets back on. On the fourth day she rides to the end of the path on her own and turns round shrieking.

That evening, in a tickle fight on the sofa, Leila shouts, “Stop, Daddy, stop!” through her laughter. Kamal stops at once. She looks at him, thinks, and says, “Okay, again.” Kamal's own father never hugged him after he was about nine. He has decided that Leila will choose when the hugs stop, not him.
observe: Notice how adults around you position their bodies with small children: standing over, kneeling, side by side.
Notice the serve and return between a parent and a baby: the babble, the look, the answer, or the answer that does not come.
Notice your own frustration when a child struggles with a task, and what your hands want to do.
Notice how often a child's stop is respected during play, by you or others.

drills.name: Eye Level
steps: For one day, whenever you talk to a child about something that matters, come down to their eye level first.
Notice how the child's face and body respond.
Notice how your own voice changes when you are no longer talking down.
Write down one difference you noticed.

drills.name: Walk Away Plan
steps: Write down the signs in your own body that you are reaching the end of your patience: breath, jaw, heat, voice.
Write down where you would put a crying baby safely, and where you would go for a few minutes.
Write down three things that calm you quickly.
Save the number of a health line, doctor or health visitor in your phone.
If you share care with a partner, agree on a signal that means take over now.

drills.name: Hands Off
steps: Choose a task a child is learning: tying laces, riding a bike, cooking, a puzzle.
Position yourself beside the child, at their height, hands near but not on the task.
Each time you want to take over, wait ten seconds and offer the smallest help that would work instead.
Withdraw help as soon as the child manages a step.
Afterwards, note how much of the task the child did themselves.

drills.name: Their Choice
steps: Next time you greet a child you know, offer a choice: a hug, a high five or a wave.
Accept whatever they choose without comment.
In play, stop the moment they say stop, and wait for them to restart it.
Notice how the child responds over several weeks.

quiz.q: Someone says that only a mother can really calm a newborn, because fathers lack the biology for it. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right; studies show fathers have no calming effect on newborns
Babies held skin to skin by fathers cried less than babies in a cot
Fathers calm newborns better than mothers, because they hold them more firmly
Newborns cannot tell the difference between being held and lying in a cot
quiz.explain: In Erlandsson's trial, caesarean-born babies held skin to skin on their fathers' chests cried less and calmed sooner than those placed in a cot. Gettler's research also suggests that fathers' bodies adjust to caregiving.

quiz.q: What did Gettler and colleagues find when they followed young men in Cebu over several years?
options: Testosterone rose sharply in men who became fathers during the study
Becoming a father had no measurable effect on men's hormones at all
Men who became fathers showed the steepest falls in testosterone
Only men who were already low in testosterone went on to become fathers
quiz.explain: The men who became fathers showed the largest declines in testosterone, and earlier work linked lower testosterone in fathers with more involvement in childcare. Fathers' bodies seem to adjust to the work of caring.

quiz.q: At three in the morning your baby has cried for two hours and you feel anger rising. What should you do?
options: Hold the baby more tightly and keep rocking until the crying finally stops
Give the baby a firm, short shake, so that the crying stops before you lose it
Leave the house for an hour, so that you can come back properly calm
Put the baby down safely in the cot, step away a few minutes, then go back
quiz.explain: Putting a crying baby down safely and stepping away for a few minutes is the recommended response when frustration rises. Never shake a baby, even briefly; it can cause brain damage or death.

quiz.q: What happened in Tronick's still-face studies when a parent's face went still and unresponsive?
options: The babies tried to engage, then became distressed and turned away
The babies took no notice and carried on exactly as before
The babies became calmer, because the parent's face was less busy
The babies immediately fell asleep, since nothing was happening
quiz.explain: Babies tried harder to engage, then grew distressed and withdrew. A baby needs a face that answers, and older children notice a parent whose face, or whose eyes, are somewhere else.

quiz.q: What did the 2020 review of father-child play by Amodia-Bidakowska and colleagues find?
options: Physical play with fathers was linked with more aggression in children later on
Father-child play was consistently linked with children's later self-regulation
Fathers rarely played physically with children under the age of five
Play with fathers made no difference once mothers' play was taken into account
quiz.explain: Across 78 studies, fathers played more physically, and father-child play was consistently associated with children's later ability to manage feelings and behaviour. The findings are correlational, so they do not prove that play causes the benefit.

quiz.q: You are teaching your daughter to tie her laces and she keeps getting it wrong. You feel the urge to do it for her. What fits this chapter best?
options: Kneel behind her and tie them with your hands over hers each time
Stand over her and give clear instructions until she gets it right
Stay beside her, wait, and offer the smallest help that will work
Tie them yourself and teach her another day when she is older
quiz.explain: Scaffolding means doing just enough to keep a child moving, at their level and beside them, and withdrawing help as they manage more. Taking over teaches her that the task belongs to you.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific child in your life, your own or another you care for. Describe how you usually use your body with them: how you hold or greet them, your height when you talk, how you play, how you teach. Then think about your own father, or the man who was closest to being one. What did his body teach you about being held, being taught and having your no respected? Describe one physical habit you want to keep and one you want to change.
reflection.guidance: Be concrete about movements: kneeling or standing, hands on or hands near, stopping or carrying on. If your own father's body taught you fear, or nothing at all, that is worth writing about, and you are not bound to repeat it. If the reflection brings up painful memories, take care of yourself, and use the support resources in this app if you need them.

failureMode: The first failure is to treat a baby's crying as a test of will, and to keep holding on while anger builds, when the safe response is to put the baby down safely, step away and come back; and never, under any circumstances, to shake a baby. The second is to stay up at adult height, talking down to a child, or to listen with a still face or eyes on a phone. The third is to take over: teaching from behind with your hands on theirs, or from above with a pointing finger, so that the child loses the task. The fourth is to let rough play run without limits, or to carry on when a child says stop. And the fifth is to stop hugging a son as he grows, teaching him that affection between men ends in childhood.
